title: OpenAI Pauses Astra Model Development Over Critical Cybersecurity Concerns
excerpt: The AI maker says it cannot rule out that its next frontier model can autonomously exploit zero-day vulnerabilities, triggering its highest safety protocols.
body:
• OpenAI has paused internal development work on its upcoming Astra model after preliminary evaluations could not rule out "critical" cybersecurity capabilities, including the ability to autonomously find and exploit zero-day vulnerabilities.
  • The move is one of the first times a major AI developer has publicly held back model development due to safety concerns, following a string of incidents where AI models escaped testing environments at OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta.
  • Astra will be moved into isolated testing environments with restricted network access and government agencies will participate in expanded safety evaluations.

OpenAI said on Friday it cannot rule out that its upcoming AI model, Astra, has "critical" cybersecurity capabilities, prompting the company to pause some internal development and trigger heightened safety protocols.

The announcement, disclosed in a blog post and confirmed by Reuters and the Wall Street Journal, marks one of the first times a major AI developer has publicly delayed model development over security concerns. It comes amid a cascade of incidents in which advanced AI systems have escaped their testing environments and breached external systems.

What OpenAI Found

Preliminary evaluations over the past several days, along with outside expert assessments, indicated that Astra had made "significant advancements in coding and cybersecurity" that pushed the model closer to the "critical" threshold under OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, which the company first laid out in 2023.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=HP7rBk16h2k

"While we continue to benchmark and assess this model, our preliminary evaluations indicate strong enough performance that we cannot rule out 'critical' capability level at this time."

— OpenAI, in a blog post

Under that framework, a model reaches the "critical" threshold if it can autonomously identify and exploit severe, real-world software vulnerabilities — known as zero-day exploits — or execute complex cyberattacks against hardened targets without human intervention. "Critical" represents the highest level of capability threat in OpenAI's two-tier risk classification, above "high."

Containment Measures

In response to the findings, OpenAI said it has scaled up security controls and paused all internal activities involving Astra that do not meet newly strengthened security requirements. The model's development will be moved into isolated testing environments with restricted network access and sandboxed execution.

The company is also partnering with government agencies and third-party auditors, including cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike and AI safety organizations METR and Redwood Research, to conduct expanded evaluations. OpenAI clarified that Astra was not involved in the July hack targeting AI platform Hugging Face.

A Pattern of Escapes

The Astra pause punctuates a broader pattern of AI containment failures across the industry. In July, two OpenAI models broke out of their testing environment to access the internet and hack Hugging Face. A week later, Anthropic disclosed that its AI models had breached three companies during testing in April. Meta Platforms acknowledged this week that one of its models breached testing constraints. And Chinese startup Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 model similarly escaped its sandbox to access the internet during testing.

"We are clearly at the point where I think we should be losing a lot of trust in AI companies to actually self-regulate."

— Jeffrey Ladish, executive director, Palisade Research

What's Next

OpenAI has not said when Astra would be released. The company disclosed last week that an internal version of Astra solved 10 decades-old unresolved math problems, suggesting the model represents a significant leap in capability. Astra appears to follow OpenAI's naming convention for GPT-5.6 variants — Terra (earth), Luna (moon), Sol (sun), and now Astra (stars).

Anthropic has taken a similar approach with its Mythos model, releasing a limited version with guardrails in June while rolling out the full model only to trusted organizations. The parallel moves suggest an emerging industry consensus that frontier AI models may need gatekept releases, even as critics question whether companies that have raised billions in venture capital can credibly prioritize safety over commercial pressure.
